pair: Review of the week · Design one garment from everything you learned

slides.coverCaption: The bisht edge, 1923: where Lesson 1 started.
slides.title: Your first A'ila Areeqa piece
slides.text: Six lessons, eighteen design moves. Today you don't learn anything new. You use it. You'll review the week, then design one real garment, step by step, and leave with a one-page brief you could hand to a factory.

slides.q: Where did Najdi men carry money, and what's the A'ila Areeqa move?
options: In a hat; a hat pocket
In the haskal, a pouch under the left arm; a slim inside pocket there
In their sandal; a shoe pocket
slides.why: The haskal, under the left arm. Move 16 puts a slim inside pocket in the same spot.
whys: Hats weren't used for money.
Sandals had camel-skin soles, not pockets.
Money went in the haskal, under the arm.

hint.cap: Think of a hidden spot on the body, close to the heart.

slides.q: Why put scent on the packaging, not in the cloth?
options: So the customer chooses, and the cloth isn't changed
slides.why: The customer decides, and the fabric stays clean. Oud in the tissue, or a scent card.
whys: Scent is a big part of Saudi welcome. It just shouldn't be forced into the cloth.
It's about choice, not cost.
Cloth holds scent well, which is why smoke from a mabkhara works.

slides.q: A trouser fabric is 90% wool and 10% elastane. What's the risk?
options: Seams can pucker and it feels like activewear
slides.why: 2–3% is normal. 7% or more can pucker seams.
whys: 10% is far above normal for tailoring.
Warmth comes from the wool, not the elastane amount.
It can be dyed. The problem is fit and seams.

slides.title: Six lessons in six lines
slides.intro: The one idea to carry from each lesson.
layers: The bisht's luxury lives on its edge. Linen is cool; wool has scales.
Real zari, hand-loom seams, thin fibers.
Fine camel hair is Bactrian. Ask for microns in writing.
Sadu and Al-Qatt: keep the structure, drop the loud color. Woven-in beats printed.
Houses solved heat; jackets can too.
Triangle vents, roshan privacy, canvas not glue, cupro not polyester.
Keep the idea and material, change the size and shape. Light matte silk for heat.
Plant-tanned leather, scent, red hidden inside. Every fiber earns its place.

slides.q: Which detail is most "if you know, you know"?
options: A big Sadu print across the back
A tone-on-tone stitched line along the front edge
The brand name in large gold letters
slides.why: The mekasar line: only a trained eye catches it.
whys: Big Sadu prints are everywhere in souvenirs and read cheap.
Loud logos are the opposite of quiet luxury.
Al-Qatt colors are beautiful on a wall, but loud on a garment. Keep the structure, drop the color.

slides.q: You want a summer jacket for Riyadh in May. Best build?
options: Half canvas, half-lined in cupro, sleeves lined
Full canvas, fully lined in heavy silk
slides.why: Move 12: half canvas, half-lined in cupro, sleeves lined.
whys: Glue and polyester: the cheap-suit combination, and hot.
Heavy and expensive, and silk wears out fast.
Unlined sleeves catch, and a polyester body traps heat.

slides.q: Turning a feminine heritage piece masculine, what do you usually keep?
slides.why: Keep the idea and the material; change the shape and size.
whys: Copying the shape keeps it feminine.
Bright colors usually get dropped for quiet ones.
The size usually shrinks: one bead, not a necklace.

slides.title: Step 1: Pick your garment
slides.text: Choose ONE garment for your first piece. Pick something you'd wear yourself.
checklist: Choose one: overcoat, overshirt, jacket, trousers or long open coat
Say who it's for: men, women, or both
Say when it's worn: everyday, evening, or travel
slides.notePrompt: My garment: a ___ for ___, worn for ___.

refs.cap: Start with a shape.
Tailored jacket.
Long overcoat.

context: Jamal is designing ONE first A'ila Areeqa garment, step by step. Each step's answer should be consistent with the earlier steps he chose. A'ila Areeqa is quiet luxury rooted in Saudi heritage: subtle, 'if you know, you know' details.
Quiet-luxury rule from the course: one heritage detail per garment, used small. Loud prints, many details at once, or obvious souvenir motifs read cheap.
Good first pieces are ones with clear construction and room for one detail: an overcoat, overshirt, jacket, or long open coat.

slides.title: Step 2: Season and fabric
slides.text: Pick the season, then the main fabric and its blend.
checklist: Summer, winter or both (Move 3)?
Main fiber: linen, cotton, wool, wool/silk/linen, camel hair or silk
Any blend? Give the percentages and why each fiber is there

refs.cap: Linen: coolest.
Wool: warm, scaled.

context: Jamal is designing ONE first A'ila Areeqa garment, step by step. Each step's answer should be consistent with the earlier steps he chose. A'ila Areeqa is quiet luxury rooted in Saudi heritage: subtle, 'if you know, you know' details.
Quiet-luxury rule from the course: one heritage detail per garment, used small. Loud prints, many details at once, or obvious souvenir motifs read cheap.
Every fiber in a blend must earn its place. 65% polyester / 35% cotton is tough, cheap, and wrinkle-resistant but breathes less than cotton: uniforms, not luxury.
97% wool / 3% elastane gives comfort stretch for trousers. 2–3% elastane is normal in tailoring; a 2024 study found 7% or more can cause seam puckering.
Wool/silk/linen: wool stops linen wrinkling, silk adds shine, linen adds coolness; Loro Piana's 'Summertime' cloth is 71% merino wool and 15% silk.

Polyester is fine when it does a job natural fibers can't: holding a pleat, a weatherproof shell, a signature nylon with a story (Prada Re-Nylon from recycled fishing nets). Not next to the skin in Gulf heat.
Linen: stem fiber, hollow, coolest, dries fast, wrinkles. Cotton breathes but holds sweat longer. Wool keeps warm with crimp; fine wool can be worn in mild weather.
Fine camel hair is the Bactrian camel's undercoat (19–24 microns adult, about 19 baby camel). Silk: light, matte habotai or crepe under about 16 momme for heat.

slides.title: Step 4: Build and lining
slides.text: Decide how it's built inside. Use Lesson 4.
checklist: Fused, half canvas or full canvas? (Only if it's a jacket or coat)
Lining: none, half, or full; which fabric?
One hand-finished touch, like hand buttonholes

refs.cap: Half canvas.
Half-lined.
Hand buttonhole.

context: Jamal is designing ONE first A'ila Areeqa garment, step by step. Each step's answer should be consistent with the earlier steps he chose. A'ila Areeqa is quiet luxury rooted in Saudi heritage: subtle, 'if you know, you know' details.
Quiet-luxury rule from the course: one heritage detail per garment, used small. Loud prints, many details at once, or obvious souvenir motifs read cheap.
Full canvas: horsehair canvas sewn through the whole front. It shapes to the body over time. Costs most.
Half canvas: canvas only in the chest and lapel; the rest is glued.
Fused: glue only. Cheapest, can look stiff, and the glue can bubble after dry cleaning, which cannot be fixed.

Pinch test: pinch the sleeve to feel normal thickness. Then pinch the front below the lowest buttonhole and gently pull apart. A loose third layer floating in between = canvas. Stiff with no separate layer = fused.
Hand buttonholes take 30–45 minutes, look raised and slightly uneven on the back. A hand pick stitch along the lapel wanders slightly; machine stitching is perfectly even.
Rule for A'ila Areeqa: coats and bisht-style pieces at least half canvas, never fused.
Cupro (brand name Bemberg, made by Asahi Kasei from cotton-seed fuzz) breathes best and is smooth and anti-static; costs more.

Viscose breathes well and is tough. Acetate is light but weak and flimsy. Polyester lining breathes poorly and feels like a sauna; it is a sign of a cheap suit. Silk breathes but wears out fastest and costs five times or more.
Unlined lets in the most air but can rumple. Half-lined (back across the shoulders only) lets heat out and still hangs well. Keep sleeves lined so the jacket slides on.
Gulf summers pass 35°C, so half-lined is the default; lining in cupro, never polyester.
Shirts, overshirts and trousers usually have no canvas; for unlined pieces, neat bound (Hong Kong) seams look finished inside.

context: Jamal is designing ONE first A'ila Areeqa garment, step by step. Each step's answer should be consistent with the earlier steps he chose. A'ila Areeqa is quiet luxury rooted in Saudi heritage: subtle, 'if you know, you know' details.
Quiet-luxury rule from the course: one heritage detail per garment, used small. Loud prints, many details at once, or obvious souvenir motifs read cheap.
Najdi women's dress: loose shapes, ankle or floor length, with embroidery. Early colors were muted grey and navy; brighter colors came later. Many women sewed and cut their own clothes.

The Najdi overdress (thawb najdi) is a huge T-shape of sheer tulle with very wide sleeves and big underarm panels, embroidered at the neck front and back. Locally called munaykhal, 'mesh strainer', because the cloth is full of holes. Worn for special occasions.
Hijaz ceremonial dress is white with gold zari thread; Asir and Jazan dress is many-colored with geometric patterns and floral headpieces.
Move 14 idea (feminine to masculine): keep the idea of a sheer open layer over a solid one; for men, a dark open-weave summer overshirt over a white thobe or tee, sharper shoulders, no embroidery.
Bedouin natural dyes: madder root for red, dried limes for green, pomegranate skins for purple, turmeric for yellow, indigo for blue.
Natural colors vary from batch to batch; that variation is part of their character.
A palette built only from these plant colors tells a heritage story with no pattern at all.
Classic bisht colors: white, beige, cream, brown, grey and black; black with gold is the most popular.

checklist: Fiber and %
Origin of the fiber or cloth (or write "ask supplier")
Trim, lining, and one line of story

context: Jamal is designing ONE first A'ila Areeqa garment, step by step. Each step's answer should be consistent with the earlier steps he chose. A'ila Areeqa is quiet luxury rooted in Saudi heritage: subtle, 'if you know, you know' details.
Quiet-luxury rule from the course: one heritage detail per garment, used small. Loud prints, many details at once, or obvious souvenir motifs read cheap.
Move 6: put fiber and %, micron (for wool, camel, cashmere), country of origin, and trim type (e.g. gold-plated silver zari) inside the garment. Only claim what a supplier will put in writing.
If he doesn't know an origin yet, 'ask supplier' is honest and correct; never invent one.

slides.q: What makes a hand-woven bisht cloak different from a machine-woven one?
options: Two strips sewn across the middle
slides.why: Hand looms were narrow, so the cloth came in two strips.
whys: Color doesn't show how it was woven.
Bishts have no hood.
Handmade costs more.
About 100 microns: the thickest here.
About 18.5 microns.
Under 19 microns, but vicuña is finer.

slides.q: In Al-Qatt, what are the amshat ("combs")?
options: Thin vertical lines between the triangles
slides.why: Thin vertical lines between triangles. The bottom bands are the kufuf.
whys: Those are kufuf, the "palms".
The name describes a painted shape, not a tool.
Amshat sit between the triangles.

hint.cap: Triangles are here. What sits between them?

slides.q: A dobby loom is best for…
slides.why: Small geometric patterns. Jacquard does big detailed ones.
whys: That's jacquard.
Printing happens after weaving.
Embroidery is stitched on after.

slides.q: Why were Najdi walls so thick?
options: Mud brick was at hand, and thick earth walls keep heat out
slides.why: Local material, and they suit the desert climate.
whys: Decoration showed wealth, not thickness.
No source mentions building laws.
Most houses were low; thickness was about heat.

slides.q: A fused jacket's big risk is…
slides.why: Glue can bubble, and it can't be fixed.
whys: Fused tends to be stiff.
It's the cheapest build.
That's canvas.

slides.why: Momme. Microns measure fiber width; Super numbers are for wool.
whys: Microns measure how thin a fiber is.
Super numbers are for wool.
Not a real measure.

slides.q: A Najran craftsman wants deep red leather. What does he use?
options: St John's wort, a tanning plant
slides.why: St John's wort gave deep red; Calligonum gave light red.
whys: The red came from plant tanning, not paint.
Pomegranate skins dyed Sadu yarn purple, not leather red.
Rust wasn't used.

slides.q: How many heritage details should your first piece have?
slides.why: One, used small. That's what makes it quiet luxury.
whys: Three starts to shout.
That's a souvenir, not a luxury piece.
None loses the brand's reason to exist.

slides.title: Three things to keep, for good
items: Copy the reason, not the costume.
Every Saudi detail solved a problem. Find the problem, and the design follows.
One detail, used small, built well.
Quiet luxury is a single story you can prove, on a garment made with canvas, cupro and honest fiber.
Your brief is a real starting point.
